status_summary: Congress funded the detention and enforcement-staffing asks in two laws: P.L. 119-21 (2025-07-04) provided 45 billion dollars for ICE detention capacity and about 29.85 billion for what CRS R48874 describes as a range of ICE operational and procurement costs, and P.L. 119-98 (S. 2, Secure America Act, 2026-06-10) provided 31.075 billion dollars for ICE enforcement and removal (including OPLA attorney hiring) plus 7.45 billion for Homeland Security Investigations hiring, available through 2029-09-30. ICE detention peaked at 70,766 on 2026-01-24 per one analyst's reading of ICE data, and TRAC counted 65,765 people held on 2026-07-11 (70.6 percent with no criminal conviction), below the Mandate's 100,000-bed figure; 183,181 people were in Alternatives to Detention on that date. FOX Local reported on 2026-02-14, citing an internal ICE memo, a plan to reach 92,600 beds through mega-centers, regional processing sites and acquired facilities, with the mega-centers to be operational by 2026-11-30; whether this was built was not verified; DHS said in January 2026 that ICE hired more than 12,000 officers and agents, with a workforce near 22,000, without a split between ERO officers and OPLA attorneys. In place of the shall-detain statute the Mandate seeks, the administration reads existing law to require detention without bond hearings for many people who entered without inspection (BIA decision of 2025-09-05); per CRS nine circuits rejected that reading and two accepted it, and the Supreme Court granted certiorari on 2026-10-01 in No. 26-104 (Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha).

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159 directs DHS to allocate or contract for detention facilities and to detain removable aliens pending proceedings to the extent permitted by law.

P.L. 119-21 enacted with 45 billion dollars for ICE detention capacity (Sec. 90003) and about 29.85 billion dollars for ICE (Sec. 100052), which CRS R48874 describes as covering a range of operational and procurement costs.

Board of Immigration Appeals decides Matter of Yajure Hurtado, holding immigration judges lack bond jurisdiction over many long-present people who entered without inspection, following a 2025-07-08 ICE interim guidance memo.
DHS reports ICE hired more than 12,000 officers and agents in under a year, taking the workforce from about 10,000 to about 22,000.

FOX Local reports an internal ICE memo dated 2026-02-13 that plans 92,600 detention beds (eight mega-centers of up to 10,000 each, 16 regional processing sites, and 10 acquired turnkey facilities), with the mega-centers to be fully operational by 2026-11-30; AP reporting cited there says ICE bought at least seven warehouses and six other proposed purchases fell through.

P.L. 119-98 (S. 2, Secure America Act) appropriates 31.075 billion dollars for ICE enforcement and removal, including facility maintenance, 287(g) support and OPLA attorney hiring, and 7.45 billion dollars for Homeland Security Investigations hiring, available until 2029-09-30.
TRAC data show 65,765 people in ICE detention (70.6 percent with no criminal conviction) and 183,181 in Alternatives to Detention; 43,138 people were booked into detention in June 2026.

The Supreme Court grants certiorari in No. 26-104, Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, on whether people who entered without inspection and were later detained in the interior can be held without a bond hearing; argument date not reported.

title: Fund 100,000 detention beds and 20,000 ERO officers; mandate detention
uncertainties: The P.L. 119-21 operative text (Sec. 90003 and Sec. 100052) was not read: the copies on govinfo.gov and congress.gov read in this review end before those sections, and the provisions are uncodified. On 2026-10-22 CRS Report R48874 on everycrsreport.com confirmed the amounts and section numbers (45 billion dollars for detention capacity in Sec. 90003; 29.85 billion in Sec. 100052, with eleven listed uses and no per-use amounts, described by CRS as a range of operational and procurement costs). GAO-26-108663 (gao.gov, 2026-09-24) states that the 45 billion dollars is available through FY2029 and that ICE received nearly 30 billion dollars available until 2029-09-30; its footnote cites sections 100051, 100052, 100016 and 100017 together for the nearly 30 billion dollars and does not tie 29.85 billion dollars to Sec. 100052 alone, so the CRS per-section figure stands. An OMB apportionment of 2026-02-20 (TAFS 070-2025/2029-0545, iteration 7) cites sections 90003 and 100052 of P.L. 119-21 as the source of a Detention Facilities line of 15,612,380,000 dollars. GAO reports an ICE detained population of 67,180 on 2026-07-30 and 272 authorized facilities by 2026-07-23; no later detention count was read. GAO also reports a 92,600-bed target in ICE documentation of February 2026 and an official statement of a 100,000-bed goal in June 2026 that it says is not reflected in ICE documents, so the bed plan no longer rests only on FOX Local's account of an internal memo and AP reporting; whether the planned mega-centers were built or opened was not verified. The workforce figure comes from a DHS statement relayed by local TV and is not split into ERO officers, HSI agents or OPLA attorneys. Not verified: weekly detention-capacity reports and the argument date in No. 26-104. P.L. 119-98 Sec. 202 bars use of its funds to place covered aliens on alternatives to detention except as required by law, but no broader formal limit on ATD was verified. The peak figure of 70,766 (2026-01-24) is one analyst's reading of ICE data. A GAO legal decision on gao.gov could not be opened on gao.gov in this review. On 2026-10-30 the Supreme Court docket for No. 26-104 listed no argument date, and the Court's December 2026 argument calendar on supremecourt.gov did not list the case. The docket shows a motion by the Federal Parties for an extension of time submitted 2026-10-16, apparently on merits briefing; as a procedural filing it is not treated as a timeline event.
